A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DUS research work with the same title and authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations on math, code, and general-knowledge benchmarks, including planner and block-size ablations in Table 3 and Appendix A.2.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds IFEval evaluations, adaptive-sampler comparisons, hybrid experiments, runtime measurements, sensitivity studies, and generation examples.

M1.justification: The core deterministic DUS schedule and previously described skip mechanism remain. v4 introduces a distinct hybrid procedure: a score-ordered spacing filter for EB/CB selections that defers nearby candidates and relaxes its minimum gap as the block fills (Section 4.4, Algorithm 1). This extends the proposed method to adaptive samplers.

E1.justification: v4 adds IFEval, extending evaluation to instruction-following requirements while retaining all six original math, code, and knowledge benchmarks. Additional model configurations, block sizes, and parameter sweeps reuse existing task coverage.

E2.justification: EB-Sampler, discussed but not evaluated in v3, and CB-Sampler become substantial empirical comparators in v4. Qwen-3-8B is added, and token-by-token and Llama-3-8B comparisons expand beyond v3's Figure 1 references into Tables 1–2 and runtime evaluation. The original confidence and random planner comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Original benchmark splits, prompting, and generation lengths are retained. New evaluation designs include Dream-Instruct and additional block sizes on BBH/MMLU-Pro, single-block decoding, threshold and spacing sweeps, IFEval budgets of 1024 and 256 tokens, spatial metrics on 150 samples per row, and timing on 105 samples after five warmups.

E4.justification: v4 adds skip-threshold, single-block, dilation-base, and level-skip analyses; sampler-overhead profiling; token-spacing analysis; hybrid-filter ablations; and qualitative trajectories across five benchmarks. These test sensitivity, mechanism, computational cost, and failures. The original parallelism ablation and fixed-budget block-size analysis are retained, the latter moving from Appendix A.2 to B.1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v4 identifies some baseline results as author reruns, but this supplies provenance without documenting repeated-trial or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 confidence/DUS scores, overlapping Table 2 entries, and original ablation results remain unchanged. v4 adds extensive results for new comparisons and analyses. For example, Table 4 newly reports LLaDA-Instruct HumanEval pass@1 of 24.4% for EB versus 37.8% with spacing, with NFE increasing from 35 to 59. Table 12 adds measured DUS wall-clock speedups of 3.9× and 5.8× over token-by-token decoding.

T1.justification: v3's first-order Markov and maximal-correlation argument is replaced by finite-order variable-length Markov chain assumptions and geometric-mixing derivations. v4 also introduces explicit optimal-estimator and planner-objective assumptions, block-wide bounds for grouped sampling, and a formal entropy-gap decomposition with proofs in Appendix C. These substantially revise the mathematical framework.

C1.justification: The inference-only, logarithmic DUS contribution remains, but v4 adds hybrid complementarity as an explicit main contribution and claims instruction-following effectiveness and up to 5.8× measured wall-clock acceleration. Its conclusion removes v3's explicit framing around a path toward surpassing AR models in both efficiency and performance.

C2.justification: v3 argues that the spacing bound holds throughout decoding; v4 says it is informative mainly in coarse iterations and explicitly declines to claim late-stage conditional independence. It discusses strong long-range dependencies, treats fast mixing as an analytical device, recommends moderate blocks, acknowledges adaptive samplers' higher-accuracy operating points, and reports task-dependent skip benefits and occasional hybrid regressions.

D1.justification: v4 adds a dedicated DUS code-access link, full hybrid-filter pseudocode, explicit default settings and parameter ranges, and detailed runtime hardware and measurement information. It also clarifies that standard DUS runs without the optional skip heuristic. These materially extend v3's existing harness, hardware, prompting, and dataset disclosures.

R1.justification: v4 substantially repositions dilated spacing as complementary to adaptive EB/CB sampling, adds Fast-dLLM and newer diffusion-versus-AR research, and explains why JYS is unsuitable for the reported comparison. The theoretical references shift from Asoodeh and Renyi to Bradley and Zhang. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, and method exposition, clarifying the denoiser/planner distinction and entropy objectives. Experimental setup moves from Section 4.1 to 3.7, and the appendix is reorganized into setup/background, experiments, theory, and qualitative trajectories. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain baseline columns and expanded comparison structure. v4 adds multiple ablation, hybrid, and runtime tables, new comparison plots, and colored generation panels. v3's Figure 2 is retained as appendix Figure 3, while Figure 1 moves off the opening page. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: Adaptive-sampler comparisons, measured latency, sensitivity studies, and code/pseudocode substantially address v3's limited evidence for practical acceleration and reproducibility. v4 also better qualifies applicability and accuracy–compute tradeoffs. These gains outweigh unresolved weaknesses: Table 7's supposedly matching default gives 16.8% versus Table 1's 19.2% for LLaDA-Base on MATH500 at B=16, and Appendix C.2 invokes conditional mutual-information decay without establishing it from the unconditional bound in Lemma 3.6.
